transcript:
Meeting header:
Title: Runtime observability deep-dive: OTEL token-level metrics & KV cache (Sierra Medical Systems)
When: 2026-03-18 15:00 UTC
Duration: 62m
Recorded: yes (fireflies auto)
Attendees: Alex Kim, Priya Desai, Liam O'Connor (Redwood) -- Dr. Maya Ramos, Kevin Liu, Aisha Noor (Sierra Med)
Shared links: Redwood OTEL guide (link: https://redwood.ai/otel-guide), benchmark sheet (link: https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/sierra)

Summary:
Brief: deep dive on integrating OpenTelemetry token-level traces into Sierra's VPC deployment to debug latency spikes, validate KV cache hit/miss behavior, and create token-level dashboards for SLOs. Also discussed sampling, span attributes, and quantization signals to surface quality regressions.

Topics: OpenTelemetry collector config, span design (per-token vs per-request), prefix KV cache instrumentation, batching visibility, quantization flags, VPC/private deployment network considerations, dashboards and alerts.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex: Alright, hey everyone. thanks for joining, i'm Alex from Redwood, AE; with me priya our se and liam on runtime. quick check on attendees?
[00:07] Dr. Maya: Maya here, kevin and aisha are with me. thanks.
[00:10] Kevin: hey all.
[00:12] Priya: Cool, quick agenda: OTEL spans model, token-level metrics approach, KV cache hit/miss instrumentation, batching visibility, then we go into config and next steps. sound good?
[00:22] Aisha: yep, that works. we're mostly seeing intermittent 300–800ms tail latency spikes in our prototyped private cluster; we want to map those to token-level behavior and cache misses.
[00:32] Liam: perfect. do you have a sense of sequence length distribution and request rate?
[00:36] Aisha: median seq is ~128, tail to 2048 for long reports, ~45 reqs/sec average, bursts up to 250.
[00:42] Priya: good, that helps. so first design question: do you want per-token spans (every token emitted) versus per-request spans with token-level metrics attached? per-token gives the most granularity but increases span volume.
[00:55] Dr. Maya: i'd prefer per-token if it's feasible — we need to know exactly which tokens caused KV misses or long decoder steps. but if it overloads our collector, that's a problem.
[01:05] Alex: tradeoffs: per-token spans raise OTLP throughput. we recommend embedding token-level metrics as attribute arrays per request or sampling every N tokens for full-span traces. also use a hybrid: per-token for sampled traces and aggregated metrics for all requests.
[01:18] Kevin: can you show an example? like what attributes should we set on spans?
[01:22] Priya: yeah, we have a snippet. (screen share) we attach span attributes: model.name, model.variant, seq_len, token_index, token_id (redacted policy), kv_cache_hit (bool), cache_prefix_id, batch_id, latency_ms_per_token. also resource attributes: deployment_id, region, gpu_type.
[01:39] Aisha: token_id redaction — we have PHI concerns; will sending token ids leak content?
[01:44] Priya: good call. we recommend hashing or using token-class labels (e.g., PII_Y/N) rather than raw tokens. or use deterministic token buckets to group tokens by class for analytics.
[01:56] Liam: also note that Redwood runtime can emit a summarised token histogram per request (top 5 token classes + hit-rate), which keeps the OTLP payload small but gives you visibility.
[02:06] Dr. Maya: about the KV cache: how granular are cache keys? we saw evictions that look like prefix mismatch, not capacity.
[02:14] Priya: in our runtime, the KV cache keys are prefix-based and include model variant + session hash + prefix length. hits are computed at prefix granularity; eviction can be LRU or TTL. in private deployments you can tune capacity and eviction policy.
[02:29] Kevin: how do we surface prefix partial hits? like 8-token prefix vs 16-token prefix?
[02:34] Priya: you can instrument hit_level attribute: full_hit | partial_hit:length=8 | miss. we recommend recording hit_prefix_len and requested_prefix_len so dashboards can compute partial ratios.
[02:44] Alex: and expose the kv cache occupancy metric (gauge) over time plus an event stream of evictions for correlation.
[02:51] Aisha: batching — we see variable batching; sometimes a single request waits 50ms for batch formation and that hurts P50 but helps cost. any guidance?
[03:00] Liam: batch waiting policy should be set with latency SLOs. for token-level tracing, include batch_id on each span and batch_wait_ms on request span. that lets you filter traces where batch_wait > threshold.
[03:12] Dr. Maya: quantization — we are experimenting with 4-bit quant; does runtime surface quantization flags in traces? we've had weird spikes after switching quant profiles.
[03:22] Priya: yes — add model.quantization = q4_0 or q8_0 as an attribute. also log numeric indicators like increased decode_time_per_token and sample_quality_score (if you run eval hooks). then you can set alerts on sudden shifts in decode_time_per_token or drop in quality.
[03:38] Kevin: on the OTLP collector side, is there a recommended sampler and exporter for private VPC? we use OTLP gRPC to our observability stack.
[03:47] Priya: for high-volume token traces we recommend tail-based sampling at the collector and probabilistic sampling upstream. export with batch exporter and compression (gzip). if you're in a strict VPC with egress limits, consider deploying the collector co-located in the same subnet and forwarding aggregated metrics only.
[04:02] Liam: also consider metric aggregation at runtime: prefix hit-rate counters, token-latency histograms, and only export full traces on anomaly conditions. this reduces network IO.
[04:12] Aisha: anomaly conditions... what's the cheapest way to trigger full traces?
[04:16] Alex: set adaptive sampling: trigger full trace when token-latency > x ms for y tokens, or when cache miss rate > z for a request. that ensures you get high-fidelity data only during incidents.
[04:27] Kevin: we need an example OTLP config for tail sampling rules.
[04:31] Priya: we'll send that after the call. (notes)
[04:34] Dr. Maya: dashboards — we want token-level histograms with overlays for quant profiles and model rollouts. can Redwood provide a starter dashboard?
[04:42] Alex: yes, we'll share a template for Grafana and the raw panels: token-latency p50/p95/p99, decode_time_per_token histogram, kv_hit_rate over rolling window, batch_wait_ms distribution, and sample-trace links.
[04:55] Aisha: how do you link traces back to logs in our stack? we use a custom trace_id format.
[04:59] Liam: include trace_id as a resource attribute; also add request_id and session_id. we can map those to your logging pipeline; many teams map via traceparent or a custom header.
[05:10] Kevin: curious about storage/cost — at our scale, token-level traces could blow up storage. what are realistic numbers?
[05:16] Priya: rough back-of-envelope: if you emit a small span per token ~200 bytes compressed, 250 reqs/sec x avg 128 tokens => ~6.4MB/s ~ 550GB/day. with sampling and aggregation you can cut that by 10–50x. exacts depend on compression and attributes.
[05:33] Dr. Maya: that's big. we need to balance observability and cost.
[05:36] Alex: agreed. start with aggregated metrics + sampled traces for incidents, then expand sampling if needed.
[05:42] Aisha: private network concerns: our security team will want to know collector endpoints and encryption. we require mTLS and KMS for any exported payloads.
[05:51] Priya: Redwood supports mTLS to collector endpoints and can integrate with your KMS/HSM for key management on private deployments. we'll provide the network diagram and cert rotation guidance.
[06:01] Kevin: deployment mode — is there a difference in signal availability between Hosted and Private?
[06:05] Liam: minor differences. Hosted can stream more telemetry to Redwood-managed observability. Private you own collectors and can choose which telemetry leaves the VPC; runtime still emits the same span attributes. in dedicated mode (Redwood Dedicated) you can request enhanced telemetry hooks.
[06:20] Dr. Maya: about model rollouts: if we do a canary, can traces show variant-level regressions?
[06:26] Priya: yes — include model.variant attribute and route a small percentage of traffic; use dashboard panels to compare p95/p99 by variant and kv_hit_rate by variant.
[06:33] Alex: also use automatic regression alerts tied to your eval prompt set; if quality drops + latency increases, auto-flag the deployment.
[06:40] Aisha: question on KV cache TTL and multi-tenant isolation — we plan to have multiple orgs in the same cluster. does prefix hashing ensure tenant isolation in cache keys?
[06:50] Liam: we namespace cache keys with tenant_id; by default no sharing unless you enable cross-tenant caching. for privacy we recommend strict namespacing.
[06:58] Kevin: okay. can we run the benchmark on a dedicated small pool? we want to reproduce the spikes.
[07:02] Priya: yes — we'll spin up a small reserved pool and run the 2-hour test with your traffic profile. we'll capture token-level traces on sampled requests and full metrics.
[07:11] Dr. Maya: good. what will you need from us?
[07:14] Priya: sample traffic profile (CSV or replay), a list of critical prompts, the network egress rules, and preferred quant profiles to test.
[07:22] Aisha: i'll share the CSV and prompt set after this call.
[07:25] Alex: perfect. also, we'll include an example dashboard and OTLP collector config in the follow-up email.
[07:31] Kevin: any known gotchas with OTLP + gRPC compression on slower links?
[07:36] Liam: if you enable gzip and batch exporter, ensure your collector has enough CPU to decompress; we've seen CPU become the bottleneck in some private deployments. fine tune batch_size and timeout.
[07:47] Dr. Maya: curious about the timeline — we want initial findings within two weeks.
[07:51] Alex: doable. Priya can run the benchmarks and deliver initial artifact in ~5 business days, full report by two weeks.
[07:59] Priya: yes, i'll take point.
[08:02] Aisha: thanks. one more thing: can Redwood produce a lightweight agent that emits only metric aggregates (no traces) for compliance teams?
[08:11] Liam: yes, runtime can be configured to only emit metrics + occasional sampled traces. that mode is common for high-compliance environments.
[08:18] Kevin: ok thanks.

[58:30] Alex: quick recap/action items — send OTLP snippet, schedule benchmark, share SOC2 & network docs, provide dashboard template.
[58:45] Dr. Maya: great. we'll look for the mail and prep the traffic profile.
[58:51] Alex: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with calendar invite for the benchmark run.
[58:56] Kevin: thanks.
[59:02] Priya: thanks all. bye.

Notes on transcription: occasional misheard words (OTLP sometimes as "O T L P"), proper nouns may be inconsistent (Sierra Medical / Sierra Med). There were a handful of overlapping talk segments around 07:00–07:20 where two speakers talked.
